The London Underground is the oldest underground railway in the world.
The first line opened on 10 January 1863.
It was the Metropolitan Railway, and it went from Paddington to Farringdon Street.

The first trains were steam trains.
Can you imagine smoke in a tunnel?

The Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco, California.

Cars came the next day.
The bridge is 1.7 miles (about 2.7 kilometers) long.
It was the longest suspension bridge in the world until 1964.
The bridge is not gold.

In September 1658 a London newspaper printed the first advertisement for tea in Britain.

In 1662 King Charles II married Catherine of Braganza, a princess from Portugal.

It became very fashionable.

Only rich people could buy it, and the lady of the house kept the keys to the tea boxes.

In 1838 104,960 gold coins arrived in America.
The money was “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge”.
In 1846 Congress created the Smithsonian.
The first building, the red “Castle”, opened in 1855.

His remains were brought from Italy in 1904.
The museums keep many famous objects: the Hope Diamond, the Wright brothers' first airplane and the Star-Spangled Banner, the flag that inspired the national anthem.

Four huge faces of U.S. presidents are carved into the rock: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln.

The idea came from Doane Robinson, the state historian.

The sculptor Gutzon Borglum started the work in 1927.

Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft.

In 1870 the day became a federal holiday.
Today people watch parades and fireworks and have picnics.

It was for patients who had trouble chewing solid food.

So, peanut butter does not have one inventor.

The bald eagle is a large bird.
It lives only in North America.
Adult eagles have a white head and a white tail.
Their body is brown, and their bill is bright yellow.
Young eagles look different.
They are brown and white, and it takes about five years, to get a white head.
Females are bigger than males.
A female can have wings eight feet wide and can weigh up to 14 pounds.
Eagles eat mostly fish.
They also eat ducks, turtles, rabbits and snakes.
Sometimes they take food from other animals.
A pair of eagles stays together for life.

It was 20 feet deep and weighed almost 6,000 pounds.
The female lays one to three eggs.

The young eagles can fly after about three months.

People shot them, and a poison called DDT made their eggshells too thin.

In 2007, the bald eagle came off the endangered list.
Today there are more than 71,000 nesting pairs in the lower 48 states.

Jefferson wrote the first draft.
Franklin and Adams suggested some corrections.
On July 2, Congress voted for independence.
Twelve colonies said yes, and New York did not vote.
Then Congress changed some words in the draft.
The Declaration was ready by the late morning of July 4.
That night a printer named John Dunlap printed copies.
Today 26 of them still exist.

The members signed the parchment copy on August 2, 1776.
John Hancock signed first.

Later, people made July 4 a day of parades, games, fireworks and community parties.
In 1870, it became a federal holiday.
Once there was an old woman.
She lived in a small house with her husband.
One day she made a gingerbread man.
She gave him two eyes and a mouth.

After a time, the old woman opened the oven door.
Out jumped the gingerbread man!

He sang: "Run, run, as fast as you can!

He could not swim, because he was made of gingerbread.
A fox came near.

The water got deeper.
"Jump on my head," said the fox, "or you will get wet." He jumped.

"Jump on my nose," said the fox.
The gingerbread man jumped on her nose.
Snap!
The fox ate him.
That was the end of the gingerbread man.

Old Faithful is a famous geyser in Yellowstone National Park.
A geyser is a hot spring, that shoots water and steam into the air.
Yellowstone has more than 500 geysers.
It became the first national park on March 1, 1872.
People formally discovered Old Faithful in 1870.
An eruption lasts from 1½ to 5 minutes.
The water goes up about 130 feet on average.
That is about 40 meters.
Each eruption throws out 3,700 to 8,400 gallons of water.
At the vent, the water is hotter than 200°F.
Rangers predict the next eruption.
They post the time at the visitor center, at the lodges and in the NPS App.
Old Faithful erupts about 17 times a day.
The wait between eruptions is often more than one hour.
In January 2025, the middle wait was 102 minutes.
The wait has become about 30 minutes longer in the last 30 years.
Earthquakes also made the wait longer.
Deep underground, the water gets very hot.
The weight of water and rock keeps it from boiling.
Steam builds up in narrow places.
Then the pressure pushes the water out.
The eruption ends, when the water runs out.

Once upon a time, there was an old mother pig.
She had three little pigs.
She did not have enough food for them, so she sent them out to find their own homes.
The first little pig met a man with a bundle of straw. “Please, man, give me your straw,” he said.
The man gave him the straw, and the pig built a house with it.

Soon a wolf came to the door and knocked. “Little pig, little pig, let me come in!” said the wolf. “No, no, by the hair of my chinny chin chin!” said the pig. “Then I'll huff, and I'll puff, and I'll blow your house in!” said the wolf.
He huffed and he puffed, and the straw house fell down.
The wolf ate the little pig.
The second little pig met a man with a load of sticks.
He built a house with them.
The wolf came and said the same words, and the pig gave the same answer.
The wolf huffed and puffed, and the house of sticks fell down.
He ate the second pig too.
The third little pig met a man with a load of bricks.
He built a strong house with them.
The wolf came and asked, “Little pig, little pig, let me come in!” “No, no!” said the pig.
The wolf huffed and puffed.
He huffed and puffed again, but he could not blow down the brick house.
The wolf was very angry.
Then the wolf tried to be clever. “Little pig, I know a field with good turnips,” he said. “I will come at six o'clock tomorrow, and we will go together.” “Very well,” said the pig.
But the pig got up at five o'clock.
He went to the field and came back with turnips.
At six the wolf knocked. “Are you ready, little pig?” “Ready!” said the pig. “I have been and come back.
I have a big pot of turnips for dinner.” The wolf was angry, but he tried again. “I know a tree with nice apples,” he said. “I will come at five.” The pig got up at four and climbed the apple tree.
Then he saw the wolf!
He was very afraid. “Are the apples nice?” asked the wolf. “Yes, very nice,” said the pig. “I will throw you one.” He threw an apple far away.
The wolf ran after it, and the pig jumped down and ran home.
Next the wolf asked the pig to a fair.
The pig went early and bought a butter churn.
Then he saw the wolf and hid in the churn.
It rolled down the hill, and the wolf ran away in fear.
At last the wolf climbed on the roof to come down the chimney.
But the pig put a pot of water on the fire.
The wolf fell into the pot.
The pig put the lid on it and ate him for supper.
After that the little pig lived happily.
